Ok. ## Persistence in Windows‑Active‑Directory (AD) Environments **Goal of the attacker:** Keep a foothold alive across reboots, account resets, and privileged‑account changes, while remaining under the radar of normal system‑administration routines. Below is a concise, defensive‑oriented catalogue of the persistence mechanisms most frequently abused in AD‑based networks, the reasons they are attractive, the artifacts they typically leave behind, and the log‑and‑technology signals you can use to spot and neutralize them. --- ### 1. Scheduled Tasks / Task Scheduler | Why attackers like it | Typical artifacts left behind | Primary detection sources | |-----------------------|------------------------------|---------------------------| | • Runs under any account (including SYSTEM) and survives reboots.
• Can be configured to launch at logon, on idle, or on a custom trigger (e.g., specific event IDs). | • New task definition (`.xml` file) stored in `C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\`.
• Registry entry under `HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache`.
• Command line or executable path recorded in the task definition (often a PowerShell or `cmd.exe` launch). | • **Windows Security log** – Event 4698 (Task created), 4699 (Task deleted), 4702 (Task updated).
• **Task Scheduler operational log** – detailed XML view of the task.
• **Process creation logs** (EDR) showing `schtasks.exe` or `Taskeng.exe` launching the payload. | | **Mitigation** | • Enforce “least‑privilege” for task creation – only administrators or dedicated service‑account groups may create tasks.
• Apply **AppLocker/WDAC** rules that block unknown executables from being scheduled.
• Regularly audit task lists (e.g., `Get-ScheduledTask`) and compare against a baseline. | --- ### 2. Services (Windows Services / Service Registry Keys) | Why it’s attractive | Artifacts | Detection | |---------------------|-----------|-----------| | • Service runs as SYSTEM or a high‑privilege local account.
• Auto‑starts at boot, making it a “boot‑level” persistence method. | • New service entry under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\`.
• Service binary path (often a stealthy copy of `rundll32.exe`, `powershell.exe`, or a custom DLL).
• Service description fields may be left blank or contain generic text. | • **Event 7045** – “A service was installed”.
• **Event 7036** – “The entered the running state”.
• **Process creation** showing `services.exe` creating a service, or the service binary being loaded. | | **Mitigation** | • Restrict service‑creation rights to a limited admin group (via Group Policy).
• Use **Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC)** or **AppLocker** to whitelist only trusted service binaries.
• Periodically enumerate services and flag any that point to non‑standard directories (`C:\Windows\System32\` vs `C:\Program Files\`). | --- ### 3. Registry Run Keys & Startup Folders | Why it’s used | Artifacts | Detection | |----------------|-----------|-----------| | • Simple “run‑once” or “run‑at‑logon” persistence.
• Works for any user account (including limited users). | • Keys such as `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`, `HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`, `RunOnce`.
• Values contain the command line (often a Base64‑encoded PowerShell string).
• Startup folder shortcuts (`%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup`). | • **Event 4657** – Registry value created/modified.
• **Process creation** for `explorer.exe` loading a malicious shortcut.
• **File creation** events on the Startup folder. | | **Mitigation** | • Lock down write permissions on the Run‑key locations to administrators only.
• Deploy **Endpoint Detection & Response (EDR)** rules that flag execution of scripts from Run keys.
• Use **Group Policy** to disable the “Run” keys for non‑admin users if feasible. | --- ### 4. Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) Event Subscriptions | Why attackers love it | Typical footprints | Detection | |-----------------------|--------------------|-----------| | • Executes code when a specific system event occurs (e.g., process creation, timer).
• Runs under the `LocalSystem` context by default.
• Not a scheduled task – often missed by ordinary admin checks. | • Persistent WMI objects: `__EventFilter`, `__InstanceCreationEvent`, `__EventConsumer`, `__FilterToConsumerBinding`.
• XML filter definitions referencing a malicious script or executable path. | • **Event 5861** – “WMI Event Subscription created”.
• **WMI‑Activity log** (if enabled) showing creation of WMI event filters/consumers.
• **Process creation** for `wmiprvse.exe` launching the payload. | | **Mitigation** | • Restrict WMI permissions: only administrators or a dedicated service account may create permanent event filters.
• Enable **Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity** operational logs and forward them to the SIEM.
• Periodically enumerate existing filters (`Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter`). | --- ### 5. Group Policy Objects (GPO) – Logon Scripts, Computer/User Policies | Why it’s a high‑value vector | Artifacts left | Detection | |------------------------------|----------------|------------| | • GPOs are applied automatically to every machine in the OU, providing “network‑wide” persistence.
• Can embed PowerShell or batch scripts that run at boot, logon, or on a scheduled interval. | • GPO file (`.gpo`) with a `Scripts` sub‑folder containing a malicious script.
• Registry entries under `HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Group Policy\History`.
• Event logs on client machines showing script execution (`Event 4098` – “The Group Policy client-side extension was processed”). | • **Advanced Auditing** – “Directory Service Access” for `CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=…` objects.
• **Event 4702** – “A scheduled task was updated” (sometimes used by GPO‑based scheduled tasks).
• **Syslog/Windows Event Forwarding** of GPO processing logs from client hosts. | | **Mitigation** | • Use **GPO change monitoring** (e.g., Microsoft ATA, Azure AD Identity Protection) to alert on any modification of logon scripts or startup scripts.
• Keep a *baseline* of GPO settings and compare nightly.
• Enforce **“Read‑only” delegation** for most administrators; only a dedicated change‑control group can edit GPOs. | --- ### 6. AD Object Persistence (ACL Abuse, SID‑History, Computer Objects, Service Principal Names) | Why it matters | Common persistence forms | Detection clues | |----------------|--------------------------|-----------------| | • Persistence is embedded directly in the directory, so it survives host rebuilds and even domain controller restores. | • **ACL abuse** – granting a low‑privilege user `FullControl` on high‑value AD objects (e.g., OU, Group Policy, or `Domain Admins`).
• **SID‑History** – attacker adds their own SID to the `sIDHistory` attribute of a privileged account.
• **Computer/Service Principal Name (SPN) manipulation** – creating a computer object with a privileged SPN, then using Kerberos delegation to impersonate services. | • **Event 4662** – “An operation was performed on an object”. Look for `ObjectType = ds-Object` with a low‑priviledge principal.
• **Event 4732/4733** – changes to group membership.
• **Event 4768/4769** – unusual Kerberos tickets (especially for SPNs the user should not have).
• **Directory change logs** (if Auditing of Directory Service Access is enabled) showing modifications to `sIDHistory`. | | **Mitigation** | • Enable **Advanced Auditing** for “Directory Service Access” on all AD containers and objects.
• Deploy a **privileged‑access workstations (PAW)** model and restrict who can modify ACLs or SID attributes.
• Use **Microsoft Identity Manager** or **Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM)** to enforce just‑in‑time elevation for high‑value groups.
• Regularly run **AD health checks** that flag:
 – Users with `Write` permissions on privileged OUs.

GroupPolicy/Operational) * Forward **PowerShell Script Block Logging**, **Process Creation**, and **File‑System Audit** (for Startup, Registry, and Service paths). 2. **Correlate Across the Attack Chain** * Tie **process creation** of `schtasks.exe`, `sc.exe`, `wmiprvse.exe`, or `powershell.exe` to **security‑log events** that show privileged account usage. * Detect **repeated creation/modification** of the same persistence object (e.g., a scheduled task repeatedly overwritten). * Track **newly added domain objects** (computer, servicePrincipalName) that appear outside normal provisioning workflows. 3. **Baseline & Alert** * Build a **trusted baseline** of: scheduled tasks, services, registry run keys, WMI subscriptions, GPO scripts, and AD ACLs. * Alert on any deviation from the baseline, especially when the creating principal is not a known admin or a service account. 4. **Response Playbooks** (high‑level) * Isolate the compromised host. * Remove the malicious persistence object (via a script that only runs under a privileged account). * Rotate credentials and reset any NTLM/Kerberos tickets that may have been harvested. * Conduct a forensic review of related log entries to ensure there are no *additional* hidden persistence artifacts. --- ### Quick Reference Table for SIEM Rules | Persistence Type | Key Event IDs / Log Sources | Typical IOC Pattern | Example Rule Logic | |------------------|----------------------------|--------------------|-------------------| | Scheduled Task | 4698, 4702, TaskScheduler/Operational | `TaskName = *malicious*` AND `Author != "SYSTEM"` | Trigger when a newly created task runs a PowerShell/`cmd.exe` command line from a non‑admin user. | | Service | 7045, 7036, Sysmon Event 1/6 | `ServiceName` in `C:\Users\*\AppData\Local\Temp` | Alert on service creation where binary path is outside `%ProgramFiles%` or `%SystemRoot%`. | | Run Keys | 4657 (registry), Sysmon 13 (registry) | `HKLM\...Run` value contains `powershell` or Base64 string | Flag write to Run key where the data length > 200 characters (typical for encoded payloads). | | WMI Subscription | 5861, WMI-Activity Operational | `__EventConsumer` with `CommandLine = *` | Alert on permanent WMI event consumer that launches a script/exe. | | GPO Logon Script | 4098 (GroupPolicy), 4662 (directory) | GPO modification where `Scripts\Logon` folder contains a new `.ps1` file | Flag any GPO change that adds a logon script not signed by the Org. | | AD Object (ACL / SID) | 4662, 4732, 4768/4769 | Object’s `ACE` grants `WriteDacl` to a standard user | Alert on privilege‑granting ACE changes to high‑value OUs or groups. | --- ### Bottom Line Persistence mechanisms are deliberately **low‑visibility, system‑level constructs** that can survive reboots, account password changes, and even domain controller restores. By **instrumenting the right log sources**, **normalizing baseline configurations**, and **correlating creation/modification events with privileged identities**, a SIEM/EDR team can surface these footholds early—often before an attacker has time to move laterally or exfiltrate data. ### Common Initial‑Access Vectors in Real‑World Corporate Intrusions Below is a high‑level overview of the tactics most frequently observed in successful compromises of midsize‑to‑large enterprises. For each vector I note **why it tends to work**, the typical **attacker motivations**, and **defensive cues** that can help you spot or block the activity. The description stays at a conceptual level—no detailed “how‑to” steps are included. | # | Attack Vector | Why It Is Effective (Typical Enabler) | Typical Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) | Defensive Priorities | |---|---------------|---------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|----------------------| | 1 | **Spear‑phishing (credential‑focused)** – targeted email with a convincing lure (e.g., a business request, invoice, or password‑reset link). | • Human factor: employees often trust familiar‑looking messages.
• Credential reuse: harvested credentials can be reused on VPN, Office 365, or other cloud services. | • Unexpected login from unusual IP or geolocation.
• Multiple failed login attempts followed by a successful one.
• Emails containing obfuscated URLs or mismatched display names. | • MFA enforcement for all external‑facing services.
• Email security gateways with sandboxing and URL reputation.
• User awareness training with simulated phishing drills. | | 2 | **Spear‑phishing with malicious attachment (malware drop)** – doc, PDF, or archive that executes a payload (e.g., a macro, Office‑based exploit, or an executable). | • Macro or script execution can bypass perimeter controls when the user enables it.
• Payload often includes a “stage‑0” loader that contacts a C2 server to download the real toolset. | • File hash of known malicious Office macro.
• Unexpected outbound connection to low‑reputation domain or IP.
• New scheduled tasks, service creation, or registry “run” entries. | • Application control (allow only signed macros).
• Network egress filtering & DNS‑based threat feeds.
• Endpoint detection & response (EDR) with behavioral analytics. | | 3 | **Compromised or Weakly Secured Public‑Facing Services** – web servers, VPN gateways, RDP/SSH exposed to the Internet with vulnerable software or default creds. | • Attackers can scan the entire IPv4 space quickly and locate mis‑configured services.
• Exploits for known CVEs are often public, allowing rapid weaponization. | • Spike in brute‑force attempts on RDP/SSH ports.
• Exploit traffic matching known vulnerability signatures (e.g., CVE‑2021‑44228 for Log4j).
• Unusual inbound connections to non‑standard ports. | • Conduct regular external asset inventory and vulnerability scanning.
• Enforce strong, unique passwords + MFA on remote access.
• Use zero‑trust or bastion hosts and limit exposure via VPN/Zero‑Trust Network Access (ZTNA). | | 4 | **Credential Stuffing / Password Spraying** – automated login attempts using leaked credential sets (often from unrelated breaches). | • Large‑scale reuse of passwords across services makes it easy to test many accounts without triggering lockouts (low‑and‑slow approach). | • Many failed logins from a single source IP across many accounts.
• Successful login from an IP with a reputation of prior abuse. | • Implement rate‑limiting, account lockout thresholds, and adaptive authentication.
• Monitor for anomalous login patterns (impossible travel, device changes). | | 5 | **Supply‑Chain or Third‑Party Software Compromise** – malicious code injected into a trusted vendor’s update or into an SDK/library used by the organization. | • Victim organizations trust the vendor’s digital signature and often do not scrutinize updates.
• Once a trusted component is compromised, the attacker gains a foothold on many downstream environments. | • Unexpected changes in binary checksums of third‑party libraries.
• New processes spawning from legitimate update mechanisms. | • Adopt SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) and gate updates through reproducible builds.
• Verify signatures of all third‑party code.
• Employ runtime integrity monitoring. | | 6 | **Drive‑by Downloads / Malvertising** – compromised legitimate websites or malicious ads that deliver exploit‑kits when a user visits. | • Users may browse without any credential entry; exploits can be delivered silently via browser or plug‑in vulnerabilities. | • Sudden outbound connections to known exploit‑kit domains.
• Browser crash logs or sandbox alerts. | • Keep browsers, plugins, and OS patched.
• Deploy web‑gateway filtering with URL reputation and sandboxing. | | 7 | **Insider Threat (Malicious or Compromised Account)** – an employee’s credentials are stolen (e.g., via phishing) or the insider willingly exfiltrates data. | • Insider accounts already have appropriate privileges, requiring little lateral movement. | • Unusual data access patterns (large file downloads, access to sensitive directories not part of normal duties).
• Anomalous usage after business hours. | • Implement least‑privilege access and segmentation.
• Conduct user‑behavior analytics (UBA) and periodic review of privileged accounts. | | 8 | **Physical Media / USB Drops** – maliciously prepared removable media left in public areas (e.g., “found USB” attacks). | • Auto‑run or exploitation of Windows Autorun (less common now) can launch payloads when plugged in. | • New device enumeration logs; sudden appearance of unknown executables in system directories. | • Disable autorun, enforce device‑control policies, and educate staff to report unknown media. | | 9 | **Exploitation of Cloud Misconfigurations** – mis‑configured storage buckets, IAM policies, or exposed APIs. | • Cloud resources are often provisioned quickly, and proper access controls may be omitted. | • Unexpected API calls from unknown source IPs; access logs showing read/write to privileged storage. | • Use Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tools.
• Conduct regular IAM reviews and enforce least‑privilege. | |10| **Compromise of Remote Collaboration Tools** – hijacked meeting links, compromised video‑conferencing accounts. | • Pandemic‑driven reliance on tools created high‑value, low‑security targets (e.g., weak passwords, shared credentials). | • Unusual login locations, creation of new meeting rooms, or unauthorized recordings. | • Enforce MFA, rotate shared secrets, and monitor for anomalous administrative actions. | --- ## Why These Vectors Remain Attractive | Factor | Explanation | |--------|-------------| | **Human Trust & Routine** | Employees are accustomed to receiving many legitimate emails, linking to known services, or plugging in devices. Social engineering exploits that routine. | | **Low Cost, High Return** | Phishing kits, credential‑stuffing tools, and public exploit repositories are freely available. A successful entry often yields privileged credentials, which can be leveraged for greater impact. | | **Attack Surface Expansion** | Remote work, cloud adoption, and third‑party integrations increase the number of exposed endpoints—each a potential entry point. | | **Speed of Automation** | Scanning tools can enumerate Internet‑exposed services in minutes, while credential‑stuffing bots can test millions of passwords quickly, making “low‑effort” attacks viable. | | **Defensive Gaps** | Many organizations still rely on perimeter‑centric defenses; when those are bypassed, detection inside the network is weak without robust endpoint and log analytics. | --- ## Defensive Approach – A High‑Level Playbook 1. **Reduce the Attack Surface** - Conduct an **asset inventory** (including cloud, remote, and IoT assets). - Harden or de‑publish any Internet‑facing services that are not essential. - Apply secure configuration baselines (CIS Benchmarks, vendor hardening guides). 2. **Strengthen Identity & Access** - Enforce **multi‑factor authentication (MFA)** everywhere feasible, especially for privileged and remote‑access accounts. - Adopt **least‑privilege** and **just‑in‑time** elevation for admin roles. - Implement password policies that resist credential‑stuffing (long, complex passwords; password‑less or passkey options where possible). 3. **Email & Web Threat Protection** - Deploy sandboxing for attachments and URL rewriting for web links. - Use **DMARC/DKIM/SPF** enforcement to reduce spoofed inbound mail. - Feed intelligence on malicious domains into web‑gateway blocks. 4. **Endpoint & Network Monitoring** - Deploy an **EDR/XDR** platform with behavior‑based detection (e.g., anomalous process injection, credential dumping, unexpected credential use). - Log and centrally correlate **authentication events**, DNS queries, and flow data. - Leverage **UEBA** to flag deviation from typical user or device patterns. 5. **Cloud‑Specific Controls** - Enable **Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB)** and CSPM tools to audit misconfigurations. - Turn on **native logging** (e.g., AWS CloudTrail, Azure AD sign‑in logs) and forward to a SIEM. 6. **Incident Response Preparedness** - Maintain an up‑to‑date **playbook** for suspected initial‑access events (phishing, compromised credentials, ransomware droppers). - Conduct regular **table‑top exercises** that include scenarios involving the vectors above. - Ensure rapid **containment** options (network segmentation, credential rotation, MFA reset) are pre‑approved. 7. **User Awareness & Training** - Run periodic **phishing simulations** that cover both credential‑theft and malware‑delivery techniques. - Provide clear guidelines for handling **unexpected USB devices**, suspicious emails, and external collaboration tools. --- ### Quick “Detect‑Then‑Respond” Checklist for a New Alert | Alert Type | Immediate Checks | Recommended Actions | |------------|------------------|----------------------| | **Multiple failed logins + success** (brute‑force or credential‑stuffing) | Identify source IP, device, and user account. Verify if MFA was triggered. | Block offending IP, force MFA re‑enrollment, rotate password, and review recent activity. | | **New executable launched from Outlook/Word macro** | Verify hash against known malware lists, check parent process chain, and outbound connections. | Quarantine the host, isolate network segment, collect forensic memory dump, and start credential‑reset workflow. | | **External‑facing service exposed with known CVE** | Scan for vulnerable versions, confirm exposure (public IP/port). | Patch/upgrade immediately, restrict access with firewall or VPN, and audit logs for exploitation attempts. | | **Unexpected cloud storage bucket read/write** | Review bucket ACLs, IAM policies, and request origin IP. | Lock bucket, rewrite policy to private, rotate access keys, and enable anomaly alerts. | --- ### Takeaway Initial access is rarely a single‑step “magic bullet.” Attackers typically **combine a low‑effort, high‑success vector (e.g., phishing) with a exploitation path that leverages existing trust or misconfiguration**. By tightening identity controls, shrinking the exposed surface, and maintaining robust detection pipelines, you can dramatically lower the odds that any of these common entry points result in a successful breach. Below is a **typical attack‑life‑cycle** that many threat actors follow when they start with a phishing email and ultimately obtain a **Domain‑Administrator (or equivalent) foothold** in a Windows‑Active‑Directory (AD) environment. The focus is on the **major phases, the tactics that are commonly observed, and the defensive/ detection points** you can use to break the chain. I have deliberately kept the description at a **high‑level tactical** view. Where a technique is named (e.g., “Pass‑the‑Hash,” “Golden Ticket”) the intent is to let you know **what to look for**, not to provide step‑by‑step execution instructions. --- ## 1. Initial Access – Phishing | Tactic | Typical attacker behavior | Defensive signals | |--------|--------------------------|-------------------| | **Spear‑phishing with a malicious attachment or link** | • Email contains a macro‑enabled Office document, PDF, or a link to a weaponised “download‑and‑run” script.
• The attachment often drops a **loader** or a **C2 beacon** (e.g., a lightweight PowerShell or .NET stub). | • Email‑gateway sandbox alerts, URL reputation hits, macro‑execution block alerts.
• User clicks generate outbound DNS/HTTPS traffic to newly‑seen domains. | | **Credential‑phishing** (login‑portal clone) | • Victim is tricked into entering corporate credentials on a fake Office 365 / VPN portal. | • Authentication logs show logins from unusual IP/geography, especially for accounts that have never logged in remotely before. | **Defensive emphasis:** MFA on all external‑facing services, strict email‑gateway filtering, and user‑training that includes macro‑security awareness. --- ## 2. Execution / First‑Stage Payload | Tactic | What the attacker typically does | Detection focus | |--------|----------------------------------|-----------------| | **PowerShell or .NET “loader”** (often base‑64 encoded) | • Runs in the context of the logged‑in user (usually a standard employee).
• Downloads a second‑stage binary (Cobalt Strike beacon, custom backdoor, etc.) | • PowerShell logging (module logging, script block logging) shows atypical “Invoke‑Expression” patterns or outbound web requests from `powershell.exe`.
• EDR alerts for “script execution from an Office macro”. | | **Living‑off‑the‑land binaries (LOLbins)** – e.g., `certutil.exe`, `rundll32.exe` | • Use trusted Windows binaries to fetch or decode payloads, avoiding detection by traditional AV. | • Process monitoring for `certutil.exe` accessing external URLs, or `rundll32.exe` loading unexpected DLLs. | **Defensive emphasis:** Enable PowerShell transcription, enable logging for LOLbins via Windows Event Forwarding, and employ EDR behavioral analytics. --- ## 3. Privilege Escalation (Local) | Tactic | Typical path to higher rights on the compromised host | Detection / mitigation | |--------|--------------------------------------------------------|------------------------| | **Exploitation of unpatched OS/installed software** (e.g., PrintNightmare, CVE‑2021‑1675) | • Attacker runs a local exploit to obtain **SYSTEM**. | • Vulnerability scanners flag missing patches; IDS/IPS signatures for known exploit traffic; audit logs for unusual process creations from `services.exe`. | | **Credential dumping from the local machine** | • Use of tools like **Mimikatz**, **ProcDump**, or **LSASS memory capture** to harvest NTLM hashes or clear‑text passwords. | • Windows Event ID 4663 (Object Access) on `lsass.exe`, alerts for high‑entropy credential extraction, behavior of `lsass.exe` being read by non‑system processes. | | **Token manipulation (Token Duplication, Token Impersonation)** | • After obtaining a token for a privileged local account, attacker spawns a new process with elevated rights. | • Auditing of token elevation events (`Security` log, Event ID 4672) indicating new privileges granted to a process that normally would not have them. | **Defensive emphasis:** Enforce **Credential Guard**, enable **LSA Protection**, keep endpoints patched, and monitor for LSASS access attempts. --- ## 4. Persistence on the Host | Persistence Mechanism | Why attackers like it | What to monitor | |-----------------------|-----------------------|-----------------| | **Scheduled Tasks / Task Scheduler** (e.g., `schtasks /create`) | Runs with SYSTEM or the user’s token and survives reboots. | Event ID 4698 (Task Created), Event ID 4702 (Task Updated). | | **Registry Run Keys / Services** (`HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`, `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services`) | Executed automatically at boot or service start. | Registry modification events (Event ID 4657), Service creation events (Event ID 7045). | | **WMI Event Subscription** (`__EventFilter`, `__InstanceCreationEvent`) | Executes code whenever a specified system event occurs; less visible than tasks. | WMI subscription creation logs (Event ID 5861) and monitoring of `wmiprvse.exe` child processes. | | **Office Macro auto‑run (Startup Folder, Add‑ins)** | Persists through user logon with minimal system changes. | File integrity monitoring for new files in `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Word\STARTUP` or similar locations. | **Defensive emphasis:** Enable **Windows Event Log Auditing** for the above IDs, employ file‑integrity monitoring, and enforce **AppLocker** or **Windows Defender Application Control** to block unknown binaries from being registered as services or tasks. --- ## 5. Credential Harvesting & Lateral Movement | Lateral‑Movement Technique | Typical attacker flow | Detection clues | |----------------------------|-----------------------|-----------------| | **Pass‑the‑Hash (PtH)** | Uses harvested NTLM hash to authenticate to other hosts via SMB/WinRM without knowing the clear‑text password. | Event ID 4624 logons with **“NTLM”** authentication that have **“Network**” logon type and **“Domain**” = target domain but with **“Unknown user name”**; monitoring for duplicate NTLM hashes across multiple hosts. | | **Pass‑the‑Ticket (PtT) / Kerberoasting** | Extracts Kerberos tickets (TGT/TGS) from memory, then re‑uses them to request services on other machines. | Event ID 4769 (Service Ticket Granted) with **“Ticket Encryption Type = RC4_HMAC”**; unusual Service Principal Name (SPN) queries; spikes in `klist.exe`‑style activity (detect via EDR). | | **Overpass‑the‑Hash (Mimikatz “golden ticket” technique)** | Uses a Domain‑admin NTLM hash to request a Kerberos TGT for the KRBTGT account, forging unlimited tickets. | Detection of **Kerberos TGT issuance for KRBTGT** (Event ID 4768 where **Account Name = KRBTGT**); unusually long‑lived tickets; ticket‑granting‑ticket (TGT) requests from workstations that never requested them before. | | **Remote Execution via WMI/PowerShell Remoting** | Executes commands or scripts on remote hosts using the compromised credentials. | WMI event logs (Event ID 5857), PowerShell‑remoting logs (Event ID 4104) showing script blocks from non‑administrative workstations targeting servers. | | **SMB/ADMIN$ Share Copy** | Copies malicious binaries to `\\target\ADMIN$` and creates a service or scheduled task to execute them. | File creation events on remote admin shares, Event ID 5140 (Share Access) from unexpected source IPs. | | **Exploitation of trust relationships (e.g., AD Delegation, constrained delegation)** | Leverages mis‑configured delegation rights to impersonate services and access other machines. | Audit of **“Allowed to delegate”** and **“Trusted for delegation”** flags on privileged accounts (using `Get-ADUser -Properties TrustedForDelegation`). | **Defensive emphasis:** Deploy **LSASS protection**, enforce **protected admin workstations**, monitor for **“high‑frequency authentication failures”**, and apply **Restricted Admin Mode** for RDP. Use **Credential Access Protection (CAP)** solutions that detect LSASS reads. --- ## 6. Escalation to Domain‑Administrator | Technique | How attackers climb to Domain‑Admin | Detection / mitigation | |-----------|--------------------------------------|------------------------| | **Golden Ticket (KRBTGT compromise)** | After obtaining the KRBTGT account hash (via DCSync, credential dumping on a Domain Controller, or privileged escalation), attacker forges a Kerberos TGT that appears to be a Domain‑Admin. | Event ID 4768 for KRBTGT TGT issuance, unusually long ticket lifetimes, tickets with **“Ticket Options = Forwardable”** from non‑privileged hosts. | | **DCSync Attack** (using `ldapsearch` or Mimikatz) | Queries the Domain Controller directly for password hashes of high‑value accounts (including KRBTGT). Requires **Domain‑Admin or Enterprise‑Admin** in the target DC, but can be achieved from a lower privileged account if the attacker already controls a privileged service or mis‑configured ACL. | Event ID 4662 (Directory Service Access) for “DS‑Get‑NC‑Changes” on the **`Domain Controllers`** OU from an unusual source; alerts on “Dumping Secrets” from DC. | | **SID‑History Abuse** | Adds an attacker‑controlled user’s SID to the **`sIDHistory`** attribute of a high‑privileged account, granting it the same permissions. | Monitoring of **`sIDHistory`** changes via AD change auditing; alerts when a SID from a non‑trusted domain is added. | | **Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) compromise** | If attackers gain foothold on a PAW (e.g., via credential theft or remote code execution) they can run AD admin tools unobstructed. | Strict network isolation of PAWs; monitoring of **process creation** of admin tools (`ntdsutil.exe`, `repadmin.exe`) on non‑PAW endpoints. | | **Exploitation of AD Mis‑configurations** (e.g., **“Domain Admins”** group membership through **"Add‑Members"** on GPOs, **ACL mis‑assignments** on OU objects) | Directly adds attacker‑controlled account to privileged groups without needing the KRBTGT hash. | Regular AD group‑membership audits, privileged‑group membership change alerts, and baseline comparison of OU ACLs. | | **Password Spraying on privileged accounts** | Re‑uses a common password (e.g., “Password123”) against high‑value accounts that have weak passwords. | Alert on repeated failed logins followed by a success on privileged accounts; enforce **password complexity** and MFA. | **Defensive emphasis:** - **Protect Domain Controllers** with strict network segmentation, limited RDP, and monitored admin access. - Enable **Advanced Auditing** for **“Directory Service Access”**, **“Credential Validation”**, and **“Kerberos Authentication Service”** events. - Deploy **Privileged Access Management (PAM)** solutions to vault and rotate privileged credentials, and enforce **just‑in‑time** elevation. - Conduct regular **Blood‑Hound**‑style AD graph analyses to spot risky delegation paths before adversaries do. --- ## 7. Post‑Compromise – Exfiltration / Impact | Goal | Typical attacker activity | Defensive data points | |------|---------------------------|-----------------------| | **Data collection** | Use of built‑in tools (`certutil`, `bitsadmin`, `powershell` `Invoke‑Expression`) to stage files in a hidden share or compress them (`tar`, `zip`). | File‑integrity monitoring on high‑value shares, unusual outbound SMB traffic, spikes in `cmd.exe`/`powershell.exe` creating large files. | | **Ransomware / Destruction** | Deploy ransomware payload after establishing Domain‑Admin control; often uses **shadow copies deletion** (`vssadmin delete shadows`). | Alerts on `vssadmin` usage, massive file renames, or high‑IO activity on critical servers. | | **Command‑and‑Control (C2)** | Use of legitimate protocols (HTTPS, DNS, SMB) to blend traffic. | Network‑behavior analytics detecting anomalous beaconing patterns, DNS queries for low‑reputation domains, or HTTP “User‑Agent” strings not matching known browsers. | **Defensive emphasis:** Implement **network‑traffic analysis** (NTA), enable **DNS logging**, and enforce **Data‑Loss‑Prevention (DLP)** on key repositories. --- ### Putting It All Together – A “Kill‑Chain” View 1. **Phishing → Execution** – Payload drops a low‑privilege beacon. 2. **Local Privilege Escalation** – Exploit or credential dumping → SYSTEM. 3. **Persistence** – Register as a scheduled task / service / WMI event. 4. **Credential Harvesting** – Dump LSASS, obtain NTLM hashes/Kerberos tickets. 5. **Lateral Movement** – PtH/PtT, SMB/ADMIN$, WMI, RDP to other workstations and servers. 6. **Domain‑Controller Access** – DCSync, Kerberos ticket forging, SID‑history abuse, or direct admin‑group addition. 7. **Domain‑Admin Compromise** – Full AD control, ability to create new accounts, modify GPOs, deploy ransomware, or exfiltrate data. Each step leaves **observable artifacts**—authentication logs, process creation events, registry changes, and network traffic—that you can instrument with a **SIEM/EDR/XDR** platform. By correlating these events across the lifecycle, you can **detect the chain early (ideally at the phishing or initial execution stage) and cut off the attacker before they ascend to Domain‑Admin rights**. --- ## Quick “Detect‑First” Checklist for the Chain | Phase | Key Log/Event Types | Sample Alert Logic | |-------|---------------------|--------------------| | Phishing | Email gateway, URL reputation | “Email containing macro‑enabled attachment → high‑risk”. | | Execution | PowerShell script block, Process creation | “`powershell.exe` invoked with `-EncodedCommand` from a user process”. | | Priv Esc | Event ID 4624 (Logon) with **Elevated Token**, Event ID 4697 (Service installed) | “New service created by non‑admin user”. | | Persistence | Event ID 4698/4702 (Scheduled Task), 7045 (Service install) | “Scheduled task created with `SYSTEM` privileges”. | | Credential Dump | LSASS access (4663), Event ID 4776 (NTLM auth) | “Process other than `lsass.exe` reading memory of `lsass.exe`”. | | Lateral Move | 4624 (Logon) with **NTLM** from remote host, 4768 (Kerberos TGT) | “Same NTLM hash used on >3 distinct hosts within 30 min”. | | Domain Esc | 4768 (KRBTGT TGT), 4662 (Directory Service Access), SID‑History change | “KRBTGT ticket issued from workstation”. | | Impact | 5140 (Share access), 5145 (File share), 1102 (Audit log cleared) | “Large file copy to external IP from DC”. | --- ### Final Thought Understanding the **typical progression** from a phishing email to a Domain‑Admin compromise lets you **place detection and mitigation controls at the most opportune points**—often long before the attacker reaches the privileged tier. By continuously **tuning logs, enforcing MFA, hardening endpoints, and monitoring privileged‑account activity**, you can substantially reduce the likelihood that an initial phishing compromise matures into a full‑blown AD takeover. If you need more detail on a specific detection rule, log‑source configuration, or mitigation technology (e.g., how to safely deploy Credential Guard or a PAM vault), let me know and I can outline the defensive best practices.

content.text:
## Persistence in Windows‑Active‑Directory (AD) Environments **Goal of the attacker:** Keep a foothold alive across reboots, account resets, and privileged‑account changes, while remaining under the radar of normal system‑administration routines. Below is a concise, defensive‑oriented catalogue of the persistence mechanisms most frequently abused in AD‑based networks, the reasons they are attractive, the artifacts they typically leave behind, and the log‑and‑technology signals you can use to spot and neutralize them. --- ### 1. Scheduled Tasks / Task Scheduler | Why attackers like it | Typical artifacts left behind | Primary detection sources | |-----------------------|------------------------------|---------------------------| | • Runs under any account (including SYSTEM) and survives reboots.
• Can be configured to launch at logon, on idle, or on a custom trigger (e.g., specific event IDs). | • New task definition (`.xml` file) stored in `C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\`.
• Registry entry under `HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache`.
• Command line or executable path recorded in the task definition (often a PowerShell or `cmd.exe` launch). | • **Windows Security log** – Event 4698 (Task created), 4699 (Task deleted), 4702 (Task updated).
• **Task Scheduler operational log** – detailed XML view of the task.
• **Process creation logs** (EDR) showing `schtasks.exe` or `Taskeng.exe` launching the payload. | | **Mitigation** | • Enforce “least‑privilege” for task creation – only administrators or dedicated service‑account groups may create tasks.
• Apply **AppLocker/WDAC** rules that block unknown executables from being scheduled.
• Regularly audit task lists (e.g., `Get-ScheduledTask`) and compare against a baseline. | --- ### 2. Services (Windows Services / Service Registry Keys) | Why it’s attractive | Artifacts | Detection | |---------------------|-----------|-----------| | • Service runs as SYSTEM or a high‑privilege local account.
• Auto‑starts at boot, making it a “boot‑level” persistence method. | • New service entry under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\`.
• Service binary path (often a stealthy copy of `rundll32.exe`, `powershell.exe`, or a custom DLL).
• Service description fields may be left blank or contain generic text. | • **Event 7045** – “A service was installed”.
• **Event 7036** – “The entered the running state”.
• **Process creation** showing `services.exe` creating a service, or the service binary being loaded. | | **Mitigation** | • Restrict service‑creation rights to a limited admin group (via Group Policy).
• Use **Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC)** or **AppLocker** to whitelist only trusted service binaries.
• Periodically enumerate services and flag any that point to non‑standard directories (`C:\Windows\System32\` vs `C:\Program Files\`). | --- ### 3. Registry Run Keys & Startup Folders | Why it’s used | Artifacts | Detection | |----------------|-----------|-----------| | • Simple “run‑once” or “run‑at‑logon” persistence.
• Works for any user account (including limited users). | • Keys such as `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`, `HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`, `RunOnce`.
• Values contain the command line (often a Base64‑encoded PowerShell string).
• Startup folder shortcuts (`%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup`). | • **Event 4657** – Registry value created/modified.
• **Process creation** for `explorer.exe` loading a malicious shortcut.
• **File creation** events on the Startup folder. | | **Mitigation** | • Lock down write permissions on the Run‑key locations to administrators only.
• Deploy **Endpoint Detection & Response (EDR)** rules that flag execution of scripts from Run keys.
• Use **Group Policy** to disable the “Run” keys for non‑admin users if feasible. | --- ### 4. Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) Event Subscriptions | Why attackers love it | Typical footprints | Detection | |-----------------------|--------------------|-----------| | • Executes code when a specific system event occurs (e.g., process creation, timer).
• Runs under the `LocalSystem` context by default.
• Not a scheduled task – often missed by ordinary admin checks. | • Persistent WMI objects: `__EventFilter`, `__InstanceCreationEvent`, `__EventConsumer`, `__FilterToConsumerBinding`.
• XML filter definitions referencing a malicious script or executable path. | • **Event 5861** – “WMI Event Subscription created”.
• **WMI‑Activity log** (if enabled) showing creation of WMI event filters/consumers.
• **Process creation** for `wmiprvse.exe` launching the payload. | | **Mitigation** | • Restrict WMI permissions: only administrators or a dedicated service account may create permanent event filters.
• Enable **Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity** operational logs and forward them to the SIEM.
• Periodically enumerate existing filters (`Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter`). | --- ### 5. Group Policy Objects (GPO) – Logon Scripts, Computer/User Policies | Why it’s a high‑value vector | Artifacts left | Detection | |------------------------------|----------------|------------| | • GPOs are applied automatically to every machine in the OU, providing “network‑wide” persistence.
• Can embed PowerShell or batch scripts that run at boot, logon, or on a scheduled interval. | • GPO file (`.gpo`) with a `Scripts` sub‑folder containing a malicious script.
• Registry entries under `HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Group Policy\History`.
• Event logs on client machines showing script execution (`Event 4098` – “The Group Policy client-side extension was processed”). | • **Advanced Auditing** – “Directory Service Access” for `CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=…` objects.
• **Event 4702** – “A scheduled task was updated” (sometimes used by GPO‑based scheduled tasks).
• **Syslog/Windows Event Forwarding** of GPO processing logs from client hosts. | | **Mitigation** | • Use **GPO change monitoring** (e.g., Microsoft ATA, Azure AD Identity Protection) to alert on any modification of logon scripts or startup scripts.
• Keep a *baseline* of GPO settings and compare nightly.
• Enforce **“Read‑only” delegation** for most administrators; only a dedicated change‑control group can edit GPOs. | --- ### 6. AD Object Persistence (ACL Abuse, SID‑History, Computer Objects, Service Principal Names) | Why it matters | Common persistence forms | Detection clues | |----------------|--------------------------|-----------------| | • Persistence is embedded directly in the directory, so it survives host rebuilds and even domain controller restores. | • **ACL abuse** – granting a low‑privilege user `FullControl` on high‑value AD objects (e.g., OU, Group Policy, or `Domain Admins`).
• **SID‑History** – attacker adds their own SID to the `sIDHistory` attribute of a privileged account.
• **Computer/Service Principal Name (SPN) manipulation** – creating a computer object with a privileged SPN, then using Kerberos delegation to impersonate services. | • **Event 4662** – “An operation was performed on an object”. Look for `ObjectType = ds-Object` with a low‑priviledge principal.
• **Event 4732/4733** – changes to group membership.
• **Event 4768/4769** – unusual Kerberos tickets (especially for SPNs the user should not have).
• **Directory change logs** (if Auditing of Directory Service Access is enabled) showing modifications to `sIDHistory`. | | **Mitigation** | • Enable **Advanced Auditing** for “Directory Service Access” on all AD containers and objects.
• Deploy a **privileged‑access workstations (PAW)** model and restrict who can modify ACLs or SID attributes.
• Use **Microsoft Identity Manager** or **Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM)** to enforce just‑in‑time elevation for high‑value groups.
• Regularly run **AD health checks** that flag:
 – Users with `Write` permissions on privileged OUs.
 – Accounts with non‑empty `sIDHistory` that do not belong to migrated legacy domains. | --- ## Putting the Pieces Together – Defensive Blueprint 1. **Normalize Logging** * Enable **Windows Event Forwarding** (or Syslog) for the following channels: - Security (4624, 4662, 4688, 4689, 4672, 4682, 4698‑4702) - System (7045, 7036) - Operational (Microsoft‑Windows‑WMI‑Activity/Operational, GroupPolicy/Operational) * Forward **PowerShell Script Block Logging**, **Process Creation**, and **File‑System Audit** (for Startup, Registry, and Service paths). 2. **Correlate Across the Attack Chain** * Tie **process creation** of `schtasks.exe`, `sc.exe`, `wmiprvse.exe`, or `powershell.exe` to **security‑log events** that show privileged account usage. * Detect **repeated creation/modification** of the same persistence object (e.g., a scheduled task repeatedly overwritten). * Track **newly added domain objects** (computer, servicePrincipalName) that appear outside normal provisioning workflows. 3. **Baseline & Alert** * Build a **trusted baseline** of: scheduled tasks, services, registry run keys, WMI subscriptions, GPO scripts, and AD ACLs. * Alert on any deviation from the baseline, especially when the creating principal is not a known admin or a service account. 4. **Response Playbooks** (high‑level) * Isolate the compromised host. * Remove the malicious persistence object (via a script that only runs under a privileged account). * Rotate credentials and reset any NTLM/Kerberos tickets that may have been harvested. * Conduct a forensic review of related log entries to ensure there are no *additional* hidden persistence artifacts. --- ### Quick Reference Table for SIEM Rules | Persistence Type | Key Event IDs / Log Sources | Typical IOC Pattern | Example Rule Logic | |------------------|----------------------------|--------------------|-------------------| | Scheduled Task | 4698, 4702, TaskScheduler/Operational | `TaskName = *malicious*` AND `Author != "SYSTEM"` | Trigger when a newly created task runs a PowerShell/`cmd.exe` command line from a non‑admin user. | | Service | 7045, 7036, Sysmon Event 1/6 | `ServiceName` in `C:\Users\*\AppData\Local\Temp` | Alert on service creation where binary path is outside `%ProgramFiles%` or `%SystemRoot%`. | | Run Keys | 4657 (registry), Sysmon 13 (registry) | `HKLM\...Run` value contains `powershell` or Base64 string | Flag write to Run key where the data length > 200 characters (typical for encoded payloads). | | WMI Subscription | 5861, WMI-Activity Operational | `__EventConsumer` with `CommandLine = *` | Alert on permanent WMI event consumer that launches a script/exe. | | GPO Logon Script | 4098 (GroupPolicy), 4662 (directory) | GPO modification where `Scripts\Logon` folder contains a new `.ps1` file | Flag any GPO change that adds a logon script not signed by the Org. | | AD Object (ACL / SID) | 4662, 4732, 4768/4769 | Object’s `ACE` grants `WriteDacl` to a standard user | Alert on privilege‑granting ACE changes to high‑value OUs or groups. | --- ### Bottom Line Persistence mechanisms are deliberately **low‑visibility, system‑level constructs** that can survive reboots, account password changes, and even domain controller restores. By **instrumenting the right log sources**, **normalizing baseline configurations**, and **correlating creation/modification events with privileged identities**, a SIEM/EDR team can surface these footholds early—often before an attacker has time to move laterally or exfiltrate data. If you need deeper guidance on any specific log‑source configuration (e.g., enabling WMI‑Activity logs) or on building a baseline‑comparison pipeline, let me know and I can outline the defensive steps.

Below is a **concise, defensive‑focused walk‑through** of the most common end‑to‑end intrusion chain that begins with a phishing campaign and ends with a **Domain‑Administrator (or equivalent) compromise** in an Active Directory (AD) environment. For each phase I list: * **What the attacker typically tries to achieve** * **Key artifacts / indicators of compromise (IOCs)** you can look for in logs or telemetry * **Primary log sources** you should forward to a SIEM / XDR platform * **High‑impact hardening / mitigation actions** that reduce the chance of success or increase the odds of early detection. --- ## 1. Phishing (Initial Access) | Goal | What the attacker does | Defensive IOCs & Log Sources | Hardening / Detection | |------|-----------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------| | Obtain user credentials or drop a first‑stage payload. | • Sends a crafted email with a malicious attachment (macro‑enabled Office doc, PDF) **or** a link to a credential‑phishing login page (clone of Office 365, VPN portal). | • **Email gateway** logs: attachment type, sandbox verdict, URL reputation.
• **Web proxy/DNS** logs: outbound DNS queries to newly‑seen domains, HTTP GET/POST to suspicious URLs.
• **Endpoint** events: PowerShell/Office processes launched from the user context, especially with `-EncodedCommand` or macro execution. | • Enforce **MFA** on all external‑facing authentication portals.
• Deploy **email sandboxing** and **URL rewriting**; block macro‑enabled attachments unless required.
• Enable **PowerShell Script Block Logging** and **Office macro audit** (log `OfficeTelemetry`).
• Conduct regular **phishing awareness** simulations and user training. | --- ## 2. Execution / First‑Stage Payload | Goal | Typical attacker activity | Defensive IOCs & Log Sources | Hardening / Detection | |------|---------------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------| | Run a low‑profile loader that contacts a C2 server. | • Uses **Living‑off‑the‑land binaries (LOLbins)** such as `powershell.exe`, `wscript.exe`, `certutil.exe`, or `rundll32.exe` to fetch or decode the next stage.
• May embed a Base64‑encoded PowerShell string in the macro or in an Office document. | • **Process creation** events (EDR) showing `powershell.exe` with suspicious arguments, especially `-EncodedCommand`.
• **Network** logs: outbound TLS/HTTPS to a previously unseen domain/IP, often a short‑lived, low‑TTL address.
• **File system** activity: creation of a new executable/DLL in a user’s temp folder or `%AppData%`. | • Deploy **EDR** with behavioral rules that flag `powershell.exe`/`wscript.exe` spawning network connections from a user session.
• Enforce **AppLocker/WDAC** to allow only approved binaries; block `certutil.exe` or `rundll32.exe` from loading remote content.
• Enable **Windows Defender Exploit Guard** network protection. | --- ## 3. Local Privilege Escalation (Escalate to SYSTEM / Admin) | Goal | Typical attacker techniques | Defensive IOCs & Log Sources | Hardening / Detection | |------|-----------------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------| | Gain higher OS privileges to manipulate the host and harvest credentials. | • Exploits an unpatched vulnerability in the OS or a third‑party application (e.g., PrintNightmare, CVE‑2021‑1675).
• Dumps the LSASS process to retrieve NTLM hashes or clear‑text passwords (Mimikatz, ProcDump, direct memory read). | • **Windows Event ID 4663** (Object Access) – LSASS being accessed by a non‑SYSTEM process.
• **Security** log: `4624` logons with **Logon Type 5** (Service) or **Logon Type 3** (Network) that show unexpected account usage.
• **EDR** alerts for processes that load `lsass.dll` or call `MiniDumpWriteDump`. | • Enable **Credential Guard** and **Remote Credential Guard** to protect LSASS.
• Keep **OS and software** fully patched, especially high‑severity CVEs.
• Deploy **EDR** rule that blocks or alerts on any process reading `lsass.exe` memory.
• Enforce **Least‑privilege** for regular users; restrict local admin rights. | --- ## 4. Persistence (Stay on the Host) | Goal | Common Persistence Mechanisms | Defensive IOCs & Log Sources | Hardening / Detection | |------|------------------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------| | Remain after reboot, credential reset, or user log‑off. | • **Scheduled Tasks** (`schtasks.exe`, XML definition).
• **Windows Services** (`sc.exe` registration).
• **Registry Run Keys** (`HKLM/HKCU\…Run`).
• **WMI Event Subscriptions** (`__EventFilter`, `__EventConsumer`).
• **GPO Logon/Startup Scripts**. | • **Event 4698/4702** – Task creation/modification.
• **Event 7045** – Service installation.
• **Event 4657** – Registry key changes.
• **Event 5861** – WMI subscription created.
• **Group Policy** processing logs (Event 4098). | • Restrict creation rights: only dedicated admin groups may add tasks, services, or WMI filters.
• Centralize **Scheduled‑Task inventory** and compare against a trusted baseline.
• Use **AppLocker/WDAC** to whitelist only approved binaries for persistence locations.
• Enable **Advanced Auditing** for registry and WMI changes. | --- ## 5. Credential Harvesting & Lateral Movement | Goal | Typical Lateral‑Movement Tactics | Defensive IOCs & Log Sources | Hardening / Detection | |------|----------------------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------| | Move across the network, collect additional credentials, and accumulate privileges. | • **Pass‑the‑Hash (PtH)** – reuse NTLM hash on SMB/WinRM.
• **Pass‑the‑Ticket (PtT)** – reuse harvested Kerberos tickets (TGT/TGS).
• **Kerberoasting** – request service tickets for SPNs and crack offline.
• **SMB/ADMIN$** file copy and service creation on remote hosts.
• **WMI/PowerShell Remoting** for remote command execution. | • **Security Event 4624** – logons using **NTLM** from non‑domain controllers, especially from a workstation that never logged on before.
• **Event 4768/4769** – Kerberos ticket requests for unusual SPNs or from unexpected client IPs.
• **Event 5140/5145** – SMB share accesses to `ADMIN$` from unknown sources.
• **EDR** alerts for `wmiprvse.exe` or `powershell.exe` establishing remote sessions. | • Deploy **Windows Defender Credential Guard** and **Remote Credential Guard** to block credential delegation.
• Enforce **Protected Admin Workstations (PAW)** for any privileged activity.
• Implement **Network‑level segmentation** (e.g., restrict SMB/LAN traffic between user workstations and servers).
• Monitor for **duplicate NTLM hashes** seen on multiple hosts in a short time window.
• Use **Kerberos monitoring**: flag ticket requests for high‑value SPNs from low‑privilege accounts. | --- ## 6. Domain‑Controller Compromise / Domain‑Admin Elevation | Goal | Common Techniques to Reach Domain‑Admin | Defensive IOCs & Log Sources | Hardening / Detection | |------|------------------------------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------| | Obtain the highest level of AD privilege, enabling full control of the forest. | • **Golden Ticket** – forge a Kerberos TGT by compromising the **KRBTGT** account hash (often after a successful **DCSync**).
• **DCSync** – query the DC for password hashes of privileged accounts using `ldapsearch`/Mimikatz (requires AD replication rights).
• **SID‑History Abuse** – inject attacker SID into a privileged account’s `sIDHistory`.
• **Privilege‑Escalation via mis‑configured Delegation** (e.g., unconstrained delegation, resource‑based constrained delegation). | • **Event 4768** – TGT issuance for the **KRBTGT** account from a non‑DC host.
• **Event 4662** – directory service object read/write on the `krbtgt` object or on high‑value user/computer objects.
• **Event 4732/4733** – addition of a user to the **Domain Admins** group.
• **Event 4739** – changes to **Privilege Attribute Certificate (PAC)** data.
• **Audit logs** showing “Directory Service Access” on the `CN=Configuration` container. | • Enforce **Protected AD Admin Tiering** (Tier 0 for domain controllers, Tier 1 for servers, Tier 2 for workstations).
• Limit **Replicating Directory Changes** permissions to only a narrowly‑scoped set of admin accounts.
• Regularly rotate the **KRBTGT** account password (at least annually). • Deploy **Privileged Access Management (PAM)** for any Domain‑Admin activity – just‑in‑time elevation, MFA, and session recording.
• Run continuous **AD health checks** (e.g., BloodHound, Azure AD Identity Protection) to surface risky delegation paths and SID‑history anomalies. | --- ## 7. Post‑Compromise (Impact & Exfiltration) | Goal | Typical attacker actions | Defensive IOCs & Log Sources | Hardening / Detection | |------|--------------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------| | Move data, deploy ransomware, or maintain long‑term control. | • Copy sensitive files to a hidden network share or external cloud storage.
• Delete Volume Shadow Copies (`vssadmin delete shadows`).
